intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome (ABERS) is caused by hemizygous mutation in the TBX22 gene (300307) on chromosome Xq21.

checks.claim: Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome (ABERS) is caused by hemizygous mutation in the TBX22 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: most importantly confirms that TBX22 is the gene underlying Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome
checks.explanation: The abstract confirms that TBX22 causes ABERS in an X-linked family, but it never says the mutation is hemizygous.

checks.claim: The TBX22 gene is located on chromosome Xq21.
checks.evidence_quote: X-linked cleft palate (CPX) is caused by mutations in the gene encoding the TBX22 transcription factor
checks.explanation: The abstract places TBX22 on the X chromosome. The specific band Xq21 is standard nomenclature added by the draft, not something the abstract states.

paragraphs.text: Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome is a rare X-linked disorder that affects males. Its main features are cleft palate, ocular coloboma, hypospadias, sensorineural hearing loss, short stature, and radioulnar synostosis. Because of the coloboma, deafness, genital anomaly and growth deficiency, it was later reassessed as a possible CHARGE-like disorder.

checks.claim: Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome is a rare X-linked disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: a family with X-linked, CHARGE-like Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome, of unknown etiology
checks.explanation: The abstract supports X-linked, but it does not say the disorder is rare.

checks.claim: Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome affects males.
checks.evidence_quote: autosomal dominant mode of inheritance with limited expression in females or X-linkage
checks.explanation: The abstract implies that males are mainly affected but never says so outright.

checks.claim: The main features of Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome are cleft palate, ocular coloboma, hypospadias, sensorineural hearing loss, short stature, and radioulnar synostosis.
checks.evidence_quote: The phenotype extends to additional features including sensorineural deafness and coloboma, which are suggested by the Tbx22 developmental expression pattern but not previously associated in CPX patients.
checks.explanation: The abstract mentions deafness and coloboma, and implies cleft palate through CPX. It does not mention hypospadias, short stature or radioulnar synostosis.

checks.claim: Because of its coloboma, deafness, genital anomaly and growth deficiency, Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome was later reassessed as a possible CHARGE-like disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: a family with X-linked, CHARGE-like Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome, of unknown etiology
checks.explanation: The abstract calls the syndrome CHARGE-like. It does not describe a later reassessment, and it gives no reasons such as genital anomaly or growth deficiency.

paragraphs.text: Abruzzo and Erickson (1977) described a family with a previously unrecognized syndrome in males. Its features were cleft palate, coloboma, hypospadias, deafness, short stature, and radioulnar synostosis. Female relatives were less severely affected or unaffected, which suggested X-linked transmission.

checks.claim: Abruzzo and Erickson (1977) described a family with a previously unrecognized syndrome affecting males.
checks.evidence_quote: A new syndrome characterized by cleft palate, coloboma, hypospadias, deafness, short stature, and radial synostosis has been described. The family history suggests
checks.explanation: The abstract describes a new syndrome with a family history. That males are the ones affected is only implied by the mention of limited expression in females.

checks.claim: The syndrome in the family described by Abruzzo and Erickson (1977) featured cleft palate, coloboma, hypospadias, deafness, short stature, and radioulnar synostosis.
checks.evidence_quote: A new syndrome characterized by cleft palate, coloboma, hypospadias, deafness, short stature, and radial synostosis has been described.
checks.explanation: The features listed match the abstract; 'radial synostosis' and 'radioulnar synostosis' describe the same finding.

checks.claim: Female relatives in the family described by Abruzzo and Erickson (1977) were less severely affected or unaffected.
checks.evidence_quote: autosomal dominant mode of inheritance with limited expression in females
checks.explanation: The abstract mentions limited expression in females but doesn't say that some female relatives were unaffected.

checks.claim: The milder or absent involvement of females in the family described by Abruzzo and Erickson (1977) suggested X-linked transmission.
checks.evidence_quote: The family history suggests either an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance with limited expression in females or X-linkage.
checks.explanation: The abstract ties limited female expression to the autosomal dominant option and gives X-linkage only as an alternative.

paragraphs.text: Abruzzo and Erickson (1989) reexamined the family for evidence of CHARGE syndrome or association. They noted the overlap with CHARGE but considered the disorder in this family to be a distinct X-linked syndrome.

checks.claim: Abruzzo and Erickson (1989) reexamined their originally reported family for evidence of CHARGE syndrome or association.
checks.evidence_quote: we decided to do a follow-up study on this family to assess the subsequent development of the patients and to determine if they have the CHARGE syndrome.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.claim: Abruzzo and Erickson (1989) noted overlap between the disorder in their family and CHARGE.
checks.evidence_quote: This family has been cited in several reports as an example of familial CHARGE syndrome.
checks.explanation: The abstract says other reports cited the family as CHARGE. It does not show the authors themselves noting an overlap.

checks.claim: Abruzzo and Erickson (1989) considered the disorder in their family to be a distinct X-linked syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: We conclude that our patients do not have familial CHARGE syndrome.
checks.explanation: Together with the title ('new X-linked syndrome'), this conclusion supports the view that the disorder is a distinct X-linked syndrome.

paragraphs.text: The family reported by Abruzzo and Erickson (1977, 1989) showed a pattern consistent with X-linked inheritance: affected males were related through females. The finding of a TBX22 mutation by Pauli et al. (2012) supported X-linked inheritance.

checks.claim: The family reported by Abruzzo and Erickson showed a pattern consistent with X-linked inheritance.
checks.evidence_quote: Re-evaluation of new X-linked syndrome for evidence of CHARGE syndrome or association.
checks.explanation: The title calls the syndrome X-linked, but the abstract does not describe the inheritance pattern in the family.

checks.claim: In the family reported by Abruzzo and Erickson, affected males were related through females.
checks.explanation: not supported by any of the 2 cited papers. The abstract does not say that affected males were related through females. Pedigree details would be in the full text, which was not supplied.

checks.claim: The finding of a TBX22 mutation in Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome supported X-linked inheritance.
checks.evidence_quote: A novel TBX22 splice acceptor mutation (c.593-5T>A) was identified that tracked with the phenotype in this family.
checks.explanation: The X-linked TBX22 mutation segregated with the phenotype, which fits X-linked inheritance. The abstract does not say outright that it 'supported X-linked inheritance'. The draft also credits this finding to Pauli et al. (2012), but this paper is Pauws et al. (2013).

paragraphs.text: Pauli et al. (2012) studied the original family reported by Abruzzo and Erickson (1977) and found a mutation in the TBX22 gene, which affects splicing. TBX22 is the gene mutated in X-linked cleft palate with ankyloglossia. The mutation segregated with the disorder in the family. Based on this finding, Pauli et al. (2012) concluded that Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome lies at the severe end of the TBX22-related phenotypic spectrum.

checks.claim: Pauli et al. (2012) studied the original Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome family reported by Abruzzo and Erickson (1977).
checks.explanation: This paper is from 1977, so it can't report a 2012 study by Pauli et al.

checks.claim: Pauli et al. (2012) found a mutation in the TBX22 gene in the original Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome family.
checks.explanation: The abstract doesn't mention TBX22 or any mutation.

checks.claim: The TBX22 mutation found in the original Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome family affects splicing.
checks.explanation: The abstract says nothing about a splicing mutation.

checks.claim: TBX22 is the gene mutated in X-linked cleft palate with ankyloglossia.
checks.explanation: The abstract doesn't mention TBX22 or cleft palate with ankyloglossia.

checks.claim: The TBX22 mutation segregated with the disorder in the original Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome family.
checks.explanation: The abstract says nothing about a mutation segregating with the disorder.

checks.claim: Pauli et al. (2012) concluded that Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome lies at the severe end of the TBX22-related phenotypic spectrum.
checks.explanation: Pauli et al.'s conclusion isn't in this paper.
